title: Scene 8: Resolution and the Ending
description: Del reads Enid's palm, Mai's departure, Viv leaves for university, and the play's fragile reconciliation.
content_html:
Scene 8: The Final Confrontation

Leave Taking's final scene takes place at Mai's Deptford bedsit — the same space in which the play opened. The return to this setting is structurally deliberate: the Caribbean spiritual world, which Enid tried to exclude from her family's life, has not been left behind. It is the space in which the family's most important reckoning takes place. The confrontation in Scene 8 is raw, painful and deeply human: Enid must face what she has suppressed, Del must choose whether to allow Enid back into her life, and Viv must prepare for her departure to university.

Pinnock stages this confrontation not as melodrama but as messy, overlapping domestic reality: raised voices, tears, silences, accusations that carry weight because they contain truth. Enid is forced to confront the cost of her strategy of suppression — she cannot control Del's choices, she cannot prevent grief or loss, and she cannot maintain the silence that has defined her relationship with her own history.

Key Fact

Pinnock's naturalistic dialogue in Scene 8 — characters interrupting each other, retreating, returning — reflects how real families argue about real pain. The authenticity deepens the emotional impact: the audience feels they are witnessing something genuine rather than scripted. This is a deliberate dramatic choice — the absence of melodrama makes the reconciliation feel hard-won rather than inevitable.

Del Reads Enid's Palm

The play's most powerful moment comes when Del reads Enid's palm. This is the play's emotional climax and its central symbolic act. Mai, who is dying, has given Del her notebook — the accumulated knowledge of an Obeah woman — and has left Del with Enid as her first 'client'. Del performing the palm reading she once refused (in Scene 1 she declined to have her own palm read) signals her transformation: she has accepted her gift and Mai's inheritance.

The palm reading is also a gesture of reconciliation towards Enid. Del is not simply performing a spiritual act — she is offering her mother something: acknowledgement, connection, a bridge across the distance that Enid's assimilation strategy created. Enid, who dismissed Mai's Obeah as backward, allows her daughter to read her palm. This is Enid's own act of acceptance — small, tentative, but real.

Pinnock places two candles on stage in Scene 8. A half-burnt white candle sits near Mai — her life and role ending. A fully-lit candle sits in front of Del — her life and role beginning. This stagecraft encapsulates the play's central movement: a spiritual inheritance passing from one generation to the next. Mai is not simply dying — she is completing a task. Del is not simply surviving her chaotic adolescence — she is beginning something.

Fragile Reconciliation and the Title's Meanings

The title 'Leave Taking' comes full circle in Scene 8. It carries at least three meanings. First, Enid's original leave-taking: her departure from Jamaica that created the displacement the family has been living with. Second, the daughters' leave-taking: Del leaving Enid's home to live at Mai's; Viv departing for university and a future Enid did not plan for her. Third — and most importantly — the leave-taking from shame: letting go of the secrecy and self-denial that defined Enid's relationship with her heritage.

Key Fact

Pinnock's most radical message is that cultural identity can be reclaimed even after years of suppression. The ending suggests that it is never too late to reconnect with one's roots — not by going back to Jamaica, but by acknowledging Jamaica's presence in who you are.

Leave Taking's ending offers fragile reconciliation rather than a neat happy ending. Pinnock does not pretend that one conversation can undo decades of suppression. Enid's grief about her mother's death cannot be erased. The racism that drove her assimilation has not disappeared. Del has not returned home — she stays at Mai's bedsit with her pregnancy and her new role. But there is movement: a willingness to be honest, to accept what was previously denied.

The 2018 Bush Theatre revival of Leave Taking demonstrates the play's continued relevance. Thirty years after it was written, the questions it asks — Where do I belong? What did my parents sacrifice? How do I hold two cultures at once? — remain urgently alive for Caribbean-British families and for immigrant communities more broadly.

practice_questions.text: How does Pinnock present the ending of Leave Taking? Is it hopeful? [20 marks]
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (17–20): Nuanced analysis of fragile reconciliation. Discusses hope (Del reading Enid's palm, Viv's Black Studies plans, Mai's spiritual inheritance) alongside ongoing pain (grief, racism, Del not returning home). Analyses title's three meanings. Links to immigrant experience.

Mid band (9–16): Clear discussion with evidence.

Lower band (1–8): Simple yes/no answer.

practice_questions.text: How does Pinnock use the act of Del reading Enid's palm as the play's central symbolic moment? [20 marks]
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (17–20): Analyses the palm reading as spiritual act and reconciliation gesture. Del's transformation (she once refused). Enid's acceptance (she once dismissed Obeah). Candle symbolism. Links to spiritual inheritance and cultural reclamation.

Mid band (9–16): Clear analysis.

Lower band (1–8): Describes the moment without analysing significance.

practice_questions.text: Compare how Pinnock and the writer of the unseen text present a moment of family confrontation. Consider language, form and structure. [20 marks]
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (17–20): Perceptive comparison. Analyses Pinnock's naturalistic confrontation — overlapping dialogue, raw emotion, no melodrama. Compares methods with the unseen writer. AO3 integrated.

Mid band (9–16): Clear comparison.

Lower band (1–8): Limited comparison.

practice_questions.text: How does Pinnock use the title 'Leave Taking' as a structural and thematic device? [20 marks]
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (17–20): Analyses three meanings. Discusses how Scene 8 brings each meaning to resolution. Links structure to theme.

Mid band (9–16): Clear analysis.

Lower band (1–8): Basic identification.

practice_questions.text: Explore how Pinnock presents Mai's role in the resolution of Leave Taking. [20 marks]
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (17–20): Analyses Mai as facilitator of healing. Obeah as genuine wisdom. Notebook bequeathed to Del. Candle symbolism. Contrast with Enid's turmoil. Links to Caribbean cultural traditions.

Mid band (9–16): Clear analysis.

Lower band (1–8): Basic description.

practice_questions.text: 'Pinnock argues that immigrant families can only heal when they stop running from their past.' How far do you agree? [20 marks]
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (17–20): Evaluative. Agrees: Enid's suppression caused decades of damage; confrontation is necessary; Del's connection to Mai enables healing. Complicates: the reconciliation is fragile; Del does not return home; grief remains. Nuanced conclusion.

Mid band (9–16): Clear argument.

Lower band (1–8): Simple agreement.

knowledge_checks.q: Who reads whose palm in the play's final scene?
What does the fully-lit candle in front of Del represent in Scene 8?
options: Del's new beginning and spiritual inheritance

knowledge_checks.q: What type of ending does Leave Taking offer instead of a neat happy ending?
The third and most important meaning of 'Leave Taking' is leaving _____ behind.
Match each meaning of the title to its significance:
right: Creates the displacement and grief that drives the whole play
Del to Mai's bedsit; Viv to university — both forge independent identities
The resolution — cultural heritage can be reclaimed even after years of suppression

flashcard_questions.q: Where does Scene 8 (the final scene) take place, and why is this significant?
flashcard_questions.a: At Mai's Deptford bedsit — the same Caribbean spiritual space as Scene 1. The play ends where it began, showing heritage cannot be excluded.

flashcard_questions.q: What does Del do in Scene 8 that marks her transformation?
flashcard_questions.a: She reads Enid's palm — a spiritual act she refused in Scene 1, now performed as Mai's trained successor.

flashcard_questions.q: What does Mai give to Del before she leaves?
flashcard_questions.a: Her notebook — the accumulated knowledge of an Obeah woman, passing her role to Del.

flashcard_questions.q: What do the two candles in Scene 8 represent?
flashcard_questions.a: A half-burnt candle near Mai (her life and role ending) and a fully-lit candle before Del (her new beginning).

flashcard_questions.q: Why does Pinnock avoid melodrama in the confrontation scenes?
flashcard_questions.a: Naturalistic dialogue makes the audience feel they are witnessing real family pain, deepening emotional impact.

flashcard_questions.q: What are the three meanings of the title 'Leave Taking'?
flashcard_questions.a: 1) Enid's departure from Jamaica. 2) The daughters leaving Enid's values. 3) The family leaving shame and denial behind.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is the reconciliation described as 'fragile'?
flashcard_questions.a: One confrontation cannot undo decades of suppression: grief remains, Del does not return home, racism has not disappeared.

flashcard_questions.q: What is Pinnock's most radical message in the ending?
flashcard_questions.a: Cultural identity can be reclaimed even after years of suppression — not by returning to Jamaica, but by acknowledging Jamaica's presence in who you are.

flashcard_questions.q: What does Enid's acceptance of Del's palm reading signify?
flashcard_questions.a: That she has begun to accept the Caribbean heritage she spent years suppressing — a small but genuine act of reconciliation.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the final position of each daughter at the end of the play?
flashcard_questions.a: Del stays at Mai's bedsit (pregnant, beginning as Mai's successor). Viv leaves for university to study Black Studies.

glossary_terms.definition: The audience's emotional response to what they witness on stage.
The restoration of relations after conflict, without full resolution of all underlying issues.
Feelings of guilt or inadequacy that prevent someone from embracing their identity.
The process of recovering and reconnecting with a cultural heritage that was previously suppressed.
The passing on of spiritual knowledge and practice — Mai bequeaths her Obeah role to Del.
The slow process of healing cultural wounds across multiple generations.

exam_tip_html: When writing about Scene 8: Resolution and the Ending, focus your analysis on the specific dramatic and structural choices the playwright makes. Examiners reward responses that connect language details to wider themes, and that show understanding of the social and historical context in which the play was written. Avoid retelling the plot — instead, explain the effect of specific techniques on the audience.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • This lesson has covered the key ideas and dramatic techniques relevant to Scene 8: Resolution and the Ending. Make sure you can discuss specific examples from the text, link techniques to themes, and embed relevant context in your analysis.
